By Colin Demarest · Oct 13, 2026

I know, I know. It's Tuesday! Here's what's up:

  • Beginning today, Future of Defense will arrive twice weekly.
  • I'll be handling the Tuesday edition. Thomas Novelly will handle the Thursday edition. I'm stickin' to my schtick; Thomas has you covered on everything space.
  • Questions? Complaints? Happy hour invites? Reply to this email.

🏭 Situational awareness: L3Harris Technologies secured a $250 million contract from Lockheed Martin to manufacture standard-range Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System propulsion. Work will be done in a new facility in Camden, Arkansas.

What else: Countless new munitions, the Coast Guard's drone buy and South Korea's hypersonic glide vehicle success.

Today's newsletter is 1,475 words, a 5.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Nuclear sensitivities
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

The National Nuclear Security Administration recently conducted an underground explosive test in Nevada to better understand and potentially identify foreign nuclear detonations.

Why it matters: NNSA boss Brandon Williams previously told me China is "clearly" conducting explosive nuclear testing and "trying to hide it," amplifying accusations made this year by State Department arms officials.

  • Beijing has denied such a regime and accused the U.S. of stirring the pot.
  • Both have signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. Neither has ratified it.

Zoom in: The NNSA test was done inside P Tunnel, cut into the side of a mesa, at Area 12 of the Nevada National Security Site, a massive reserve northwest of Las Vegas.

  • It relied on chemical high explosives and radiotracers. Data collected from the trial will refine detection models and algorithms, according to the administration.
  • "Detection is only as credible as the data behind it," Fuse founder JC Btaiche told me.

Context: This type of work is critical "to strengthening our ability to detect low-yield nuclear tests, an essential component of U.S. nuclear nonproliferation and national security efforts," Frank Rose, a former NNSA deputy, told me.

  • Such trials, he added, "are the product of many years of sustained scientific, technical, and policy work across multiple administrations."

Flashback: President Trump last fall ordered the U.S. to resume nuclear testing equal to Russia and China.

  • Few details followed — and questions remain about whether he was addressing the Energy Department or the Defense Department. (The latter conducts missile flight tests.)

Zoom out: American and Russian nuclear arsenals dwarf all others; Washington and Moscow together wield some 90% of the world's warheads.

  • China, meanwhile, is undertaking a historic buildout.
  • Just a small portion of these weapons could devastate life on Earth.

The bottom line: A former U.S. official described the NNSA test to me as "keeping a thumb on PRC."

Go deeper: Russian nuke threats signal "weakness," NNSA boss says
 
 
2. Corps eyes U-Hawk
 

The front of the U-Hawk. Screenshot: Lockheed Martin/via YouTube
 

The U.S. Marine Corps is "very interested" in the U-Hawk, a cockpitless, cargo-hauling variant of the Black Hawk helicopter, Sikorsky chief Richard Benton told me.

Why it matters: The military autonomy boom times continue — and are service-agnostic.

Catch up quick: Sikorsky, a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin, unveiled the U-Hawk at the Association of the U.S. Army conference last October. It's expected to fly for the first time this year.

  • "This has really been: 'Hey, we're going to build it because we think you need it,' and having it available will create the need or the demand," Benton said.
  • "And that's what we've been seeing."

Zoom in: The U-Hawk prototype is based on an older UH-60L, also known as Lima.

  • Designed to shuttle tons of materiel, including drones, rockets or ground robotics, its cockpit was traded for storage space and its nose now opens with clamshell doors and a ramp.
  • "You want to have metal-on-metal contact, or you don't want to put people in harm's way? It works for that," Benton said. "But it's quickly evolved to: 'I need to move stuff, and I need to move it en masse.'"

The intrigue: There are also plans to convert UH-60Ms, or Mikes. Physical conversion kits are also on the table.

The bottom line: "We don't have a version with the Marine gray on it yet," Benton said, "but I do anticipate there will be a Marine gray U-Hawk very soon."

Go deeper: Overland AI unveils autonomous Ibex vehicle
 
 
3. AUSA weapons
 

The Tyr munition. Photo: Courtesy of Heaviside Industries
 

The annual Association of the U.S. Army bonanza is underway, and defense contractors are unveiling new weapons, countermeasures and milestones.

Why it matters: Companies save big announcements for big shows. This year is no exception.

Here's some of what's caught my eye:

🧨 Heaviside Industries, which recently raised $60 million, rolled out Tyr, its first in a line of precision munitions.

  • It works with four Nammo warheads, including anti-tank and anti-personnel variants, can fly for more than an hour and hits speeds greater than 150 mph.

🔥 Raytheon, part of RTX, discussed Coyote Block 2C+RM, which involves a rocket motor and other improvements for the widely used interceptor.

  • "You get upgraded propulsion for faster launch and higher-velocity flight, and with the seeker-warhead it really gets after the more cutting-edge drone capabilities we're seeing from the adversary," Tom Laliberty, president of land and air defense systems, told reporters.

🚀 Chaos Industries, valued north of $4 billion, debuted Vespid, a line of cheap interceptors that work with its existing multistatic radar systems.

  • The company said it can initially produce 12,000 and push those numbers much higher depending on demand.

🦈 Anduril Industries uncloaked Steelfin, a reconfigurable, two-stage surface-to-air missile the neo-prime said is compatible with Patriot launchers, the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System and the Typhon mid-range capability.

  • "The intent is to build most of the subassemblies and content at Arsenal-1, and then do the final integration with a handful of our partners," Steve Milano, Anduril's senior director of missiles, told reporters.

🛜 Leonardo DRS announced initial production of the C-Band Extended Multi-Mission Hemispheric Radar.

  • The cxMHR, as it's abbreviated, is designed to detect, identify and track multiple ballistic and cruise missiles, rockets and drones at the same time. It can be deployed on a single vehicle.

4. ICYMI 1.0: Gallatin gains
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

Gallatin AI raised a $50 million Series A, with defense-tech frequent fliers 8VC and Silent Ventures pitching in, CEO Woody Glier told me.

Why it matters: This isn't another drone builder. The California startup is, instead, focused on digitizing and streamlining the nitty-gritty of military logistics and sustainment.

  • "A lot of the logistics data that is generated today is very manual," Glier said. "It's very messy — literally like clipboard and pen and paper."

The big picture: The Pentagon considers contested logistics — getting bullets, blood, fuel, food and more to their destinations, especially under fire — a critical technology area. Others include biomanufacturing and hypersonic weapons.

Catch up quick: Gallatin's Navigator, an AI-powered tool that provides sustainment insights and supply distribution planning, is being used by U.S. military units around the world.

Read the full story.
 
 
5. ICYMI 2.0: Cashing in
By Natalie Breymeyer and Colin Demarest
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Defense tech investment continues to expand, in dollars raised and in the types of companies getting funded, per new PitchBook data.

The big picture: Third-quarter data underscore the maturation of the sector, as it spreads out beyond physical projects to software and more.

By the numbers: Globally, defense-tech VC has reached $67.4 billion across 726 deals so far this year, with $27.2 billion in Q3 alone.

Read the full Pro Deals story.
 
 
6. Quick hits
 

An MQ-9B long-range drone. Photo: U.S. Coast Guard
 

🇺🇸 The U.S. Coast Guard is buying four General Atomics-made MQ-9B drones and related equipment for almost $248 million. The contract is through Customs and Border Protection.

  • Why it matters: "This investment will give Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain, helping them detect threats earlier," Anthony Antognoli, assistant commandant and program executive officer for robotics and autonomous systems, said in a statement.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: The Coast Guard's unmanned strategy is worth rereading.

✈️ The "script has flipped on power projection" and adversaries "no longer need comparable forces to hold American bases at risk," Hidden Level chief executive Jeff Cole told me in a recent conversation. "The most capable aircraft in the world simply cannot project power if they are vulnerable on the ground."

  • Why it matters: Ukraine's Spiderweb operation was not a one-off. In fact, it's a source of inspiration for would-be attackers.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Tectonic has a great recent rundown on Hidden Level here.

📡 Israel Aerospace Industries unveiled Point@Air, an aerostat-based radar for long-range surveillance. It's based on the ELM-2083.

  • Why it matters: Elevation has its benefits. "Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense," IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said in a statement.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Aerostats (blimps!) deserve more love.
 
 
7. Check this out
 

Splashdown! Photo: Courtesy of the South Korean Presidential Office
 

South Korea successfully test-launched a domestically developed HGV Oct. 8.

  • Images, via the Blue House, can be found here.
  • Additional details, via a readout, can be found here.

The big picture: President Lee Jae Myung observed the trial.

  • "Our security is secured through our own strength," he said in a translated statement.
